# Copper April 2012 

- Following several months of directionless trading, range bound copper finally succumbed to a meaningful price shift with cash quotes heading lower from the middle of April on what was perceived as disappointing Chinese trade and economic data.  The data was of course the symptom (of weak Chinese demand) and not the cause but it was ultimately concern over the strength and timing of an upturn in consumption from the world’s biggest consumer of the red metal that pulled prices lower. 

- Our forecasts assume improving Chinese demand over the second half of this year, but given that we also predict increased mine supply, we do expect a surplus to emerge over the final quarter of this year.  As such, we now expect prices to peak in the third quarter at $8700/t before easing into Q4.  Our full year forecast has also been dragged lower and now stands at $8,477/t. 

- Global demand conditions continue to vary by region and indeed, slower than expected activity in one country in particular has prompted us to trim our global growth estimate for this year.  A weaker than anticipated start to the year in China has forced us to cut our estimate for growth there to 7% from 8% previously, which has dragged down our global growth forecast for 2012 to 3.2% from 3.7% last month. 

- During April, representative spot selling terms from miners to traders were $25/t and 2.5c/lb, fractionally lower than the previous month.  At first sight, the sharp numbers being paid to miners by the trade would indicate a particularly tight concentrates market, however, the significant difference between buying and selling terms and the limited opportunity for traders to bridge this gap through the spreads would suggest that other factors are also at play.  With Chinese demand suppressed by a particularly unfavourable price arbitrage and high stocks of refined metal, spot concentrate market activity of late is thought to have been primarily driven by traders looking to secure clean material for blending or packaging purposes.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

Following several months of directionless trading, range bound copper finally succumbed to a mean

ingful price shift with cash quotes heading lower from the middle of April on what was perceived as disappointing Chinese trade and economic data.  The data was of course the symptom (of weak Chinese demand) and not the cause but it was ultimately concern over the strength and timing of an upturn in consumption from the world’s biggest consumer of the red metal that pulled prices lower. 

The big question hanging over the copper market over the past few months has concerned the nature of the trigger that would lead prices out of the tight trading range $200/t either side of $8400/t where cash quotes have hovered since the start of February.  There had been a lack of conviction from both bulls and bears until the middle of this month when traders on the LME returned from the Easter break to pull prices lower on a combination of factors.  Stronger than expected cathode imports into China was taken as a negative signal for prices as they only served to add to already bloated inventories in the face of dreary demand.  This, combined with higher than anticipated inflation data caused prices to move lower to register their sharpest daily fall this year, down by some 4%.  Cash quotes were already under pressure following the sluggish tone to US jobs data released when the LME was closed on the previous Friday but the Chinese data intensified negative sentiment to result in prices oozing red.  Whether this fall to the $8000/t level truly constitutes a decisive move lower is open to question but the fact that prices failed to get any boost at all from a consensus forming on weaker supply prospects this year during the industry’s annual gathering for CESCO week was perhaps instructive. 

The other focus of debate in Santiago was concern over Chinese demand.  With expectations for a relatively sluggish year for consumption in the rest of the world, all eyes remain on China but thus far, neither demand has bounced back from the New Year lull nor have imports moved lower in line with expectations.  Chinese imports have been touted to fall in each month so far this year but have defied a negative arbitrage and sluggish demand conditions to keep on running higher, up by a further 80% year on year in March to 345.7kt.  In normal circumstances a strong import figure into China ought to be supportive of prices but as we noted last month, imports are simply piling up in warehouses, whether they be on exchange or in bonded warehouses.  A major part of the explanation for this is copper’s use as a financing vehicle amid continued tight credit conditions, which is also impacting the copper market in other ways as we discuss below. Crucially, net imports will need to turn lower and demand will have to improve significantly in order for Chinese stocks to be drawn down sufficiently to support the next phase of price appreciation for copper.  Ironically, the first trigger for this next phase will most likely be an increase in Chinese imports but the copper market finds it

self in the perverse situation where it needs metal imports to decline in the hope that they will increase later on the back of strengthened demand. **A squeeze is on** The other ways that China’s use of copper for financing is impacting the copper market relates to this material being hedged to reduce exposure to price movements. Given that holding material makes one long copper, this needs to be sold short in order to mitigate price risk. However, with stocks as low as 252kt and as much as 40% of these warrants already cancelled, it is rumoured that the Chinese who are said to be shorting the market are getting squeezed, with a major trading house reportedly holding most of the aces on the long side. This has resulted in the backwardation on closing prices, which was around $20-30/t in March, flaring out to $108/t on the 24th of April. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 900 12000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - April 2012 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **European premia edge lower but remain elevated** The squeeze on the LME means that premia remain elevated in Europe where material is required, although it must be noted that it was not just the lack of LME inventory that was initially driving strength in premia. Indeed, part of the reason for the appetite for spot material was delayed shipments into Europe and with this material having now arrived, premia have edged lower over the past month. Another aspect to tightness as we discussed last month was caused by semis producers having to top up their contracted orders this year after demand in general proved to be better than expected. Although the flow of material has now eased, we understand that some semis producers missed out on orders as they were unable to source the cathode in a timely fashion. This must have proved particularly disappointing for those mills desperate to fill their capacity and with orders on hand but unable to accept them because of a lack of raw material. Those producers with some spare cathode were able to pick up a few unexpected orders as a result. Meanwhile, in China some very modest restocking on price dips by semis producers resulted in a narrowing in the range at which premia were quoted, with the bottom moving higher and as a consequence imported cathode is now available at $40-50/t compared to the $20-50/t range quoted last month. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 180 10

**Stocks shock as slide stops** The almost uninterrupted decline in LME inventories over the past half a year had been arrested during the past month, although this proved only temporary as stocks continued on their downward spiral by the end of April. At the time of writing total LME inventories stand at 252kt, down slightly from March, with a firm boost in Asian stocks, backed up by a modest increase in Europe, ultimately overpowered by a heavier decline in US inventories. The decline in cancelled warrants last month coincided with the increase in stocks this month but cancellations have now reversed their decline and increased from 83kt at the end of March to 108kt now. Cancellations as a percentage of total inventory breached 40%, their highest share in eight years and point to tightness on the LME which is underlined by the backwardation. COMEX showed a similar pattern to the LME, with stocks also moving lower through the month. Interestingly, in China, SHFE registered inventories also began to decline after peaking in the current cycle at 222kt and now stand at 205kt. However, bonded warehouse stocks have continued to build, now up to as much as 700kt from 650kt the prior month although at least the rate of increase has slowed. Meanwhile, a tightening of the spreads on the Shanghai exchange suggest that a good deal of these stocks, which were built up from robust Chinese imports, are not available to the market as they are tied up in financing deals. **Chinese imports stubbornly high** As we move through 2012 the market’s calls for Chinese imports to turn lower “next month” have been pushed back sequentially as have expectations of the timing of peak prices this year. The release of trade data for March, down by 8% month on month but up an eye watering 80% year on year to 345.7kt, was not the slowdown that market watchers were hoping for given sluggish demand in China. That said there has been some improvement in Chinese demand on a month-on-month basis, although this was not at the levels anticipated given the time of year and as a consequence any year-on-year comparisons remain unfavourable. Net imports did slow more appreciably, however, with exports jumping to 26.5kt from 0.7kt the prior month as material moved from China to Asian LME warehouses supported by both the backwardation on the LME and the SHFE- LME arbitrage. However, once again the supply side has disappointed. First quarter production results from a number of miners were worse than expected and as a result the deficit has grown larger rather than smaller, although this does not mean a higher price forecast. Conversely, we have been forced to cut our price forecast for this year to $8477/t from $8700/t previously as a result of a lower first quarter average than forecast and our expectations for softer LME prices through Q2 in the face of uncertain Chinese demand and following the downward trend in prices in April. However, given the large dominant position on the LME, we would also expect to see increased price volatility in the coming weeks. As such, we now expect prices to peak in the third quarter at $8700/t before easing into Q4. lobal growth forecast for 2012 to 3.2% from 3.7% last month. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**European demand levels off** After a very good start to the year relative to expectations at the end of 2011, improvements in refined demand in Europe have now levelled off.  However, given the differences in demand conditions across the region it is difficult to sum up Europe in one sentence.  Broadly speaking, end use consumption is doing better in the north of the region, although even in power house Germany early signs of a slowdown are emerging.  In the south of Europe, conditions remain lacklustre, with sluggish construction markets continuing to cast a dark pall over order books. 

**Economic data underscores German concerns** The release of PMI data for Europe underlined concerns over the near term outlook for Germany after falling at a faster than expected rate.  The manufacturing PMI for Germany in April came in at 46.3, well below the neutral 50 level and a further deterioration from the prior month.  This was also a near three year low back to the days of the credit crunch.  More worryingly, Germany’s data was in line with Europe as a whole, which came in at 46.0.  Previously Germany had been propping up the European number.  The European data also weakened from the prior month but the pace of decline accelerated.  As such, the gloomy near term economic backdrop raises further concerns over economic activity and thus, demand for copper products. 

**Transport leads from the front** The one market that does seem to be doing well across the region is transport, with Germany leading strength in the automotive sector, in part because of exports to emerging markets.  Indeed, German production has held up relatively well in the face of sluggish European sales, with their premium marques boosting consumption due to their high copper intensity.  However, construction does remain the weak spot for European demand, although it is fair to say that some countries are worse than others.  In line with consumption patterns in general, this weakness continues to be felt most acutely in the south of Europe and in particular in Italy and Spain. 

**Infrastructure projects power up** Despite the flattening off in demand that we described above, not all sectors have performed in this way, with the power sector showing some improvement this month.  A number of new projects are coming through and this has led to an upturn in demand from this key sector.  Meanwhile, wind power continues to be the hot segment of this sector overall, with new installations both on and off shore providing a lift to demand. 

**Contraction reiterated for Europe** For the year as a whole we maintain our negative view on European demand and reiterate our forecast of a 1% contraction.  Despite a relatively upbeat start to the year, the uncertain economic backdrop certainly gives us no reason to increase our forecast but possibly increases downside risk given recent developments in Germany.  W

e are not overly optimistic of the chances for significant improvement next year either and it is not until 2014 that we expect to see demand turn notably higher. ### **Americas** **Rod output returns to October 2008 levels** It is not often that we can say that a return to the past is a good thing for metals. But US copper rod output for March of 117.3kt (metric), according to data from the American Bureau of Metals Statistics, was the highest for a single month since October 2008’s 123.5kt, and reinforces our prior commentary of a strengthening American copper market. While we would be the first to agree that this does not automatically mean a consistent return to pre-economic collapse levels, conversations we have held since the turn of the year have elicited a consistently optimistic tone. That is, even if neither 2007 nor 2008 production and demand levels can be regarded as “representative” of the US copper market, there has been a sustained, gradual recovery of business activity since Q1 2009. Copper rod shipment levels have also matched output, with the end-March higher rod inventories (27.8kt vs. February’s 22.9kt) being accounted for by stronger rates of production and material in transit, rather than representing an increasing proportion of unsold material. Furthermore, imports of rod remained subdued for the first two months of the year, averaging 10kt/month vs. 12kt/m for last year; Russian material has not been seen in the market since the flood of almost 28kt came into the US between May-November last year, and US exports were up marginally, to an average of 11.5kt/m vs. 10.7kt/m for last year. **Premia up on tighter supplies** Again, according to the ABMS, cathode stocks at rod mills at the end of March fell quite markedly to under 20kt vs. 27.3kt a month prior. It was this reported tightening of cathode supplies that has been behind another strengthening of metal premia: early in the month, material delivered mid-west was averaging 5.5-6.0c/lb, vs. the 5.25-5.75c/lb range we saw last month, while reportedly north east premia have been between 6.75-7.25c/lb, up from 6c/lb. Indirectly, tightening aluminium rod supplies in the northeastern region could be contributing to the higher premia there. Two smelters and rod mills in Quebec and upper New York state (Alma and Massena) have endured lengthy stoppages and output disruption, forcing local users to turn to imports of aluminium rod. Although much of this aluminium rod ends up in electrical transmission, it could be that other, smaller-scale users which coul

d switch to copper are doing so, adding to the pressure on copper rod availability. 

**Encore Wire dollar sales held back by lower spreads, price volatility** Despite the overall improvement at the national rod production and sales level, copper price volatility and lower prices during the first quarter created challenges across the sector.  In its Q1 financial report, Encore Wire, the sole regional publicly-traded pure play rod-to-wire producer, commented that unit volumes in terms of copper contained in wire sold were unchanged from Q1 2011, which were up themselves by 29% on the prior year, and up by 8.7% on Q4 2011.  Net sales of $280.5M and income ($6.7M) were down on Q1 2011’s $303.4M and $10.7M due largely to the 9.7% lower selling price of wire tied to Comex tags. But the company remains positive despite its exposure to the construction and building wire markets, given the noted lean inventories at the electrical distribution customer level.  Encore Wire will also broaden its product range into aluminium wire and cable for building applications by late-2012 under an investment plan costing between $25-30M. Encore will buy in aluminium wire rod for downstream drawing initially, but may consider upstream melting capability at a later date. 

**General Cable returns to US building wire market, and expands in Brazil** Elsewhere in the wire products sector, General Cable – which will post its Q1 results on May 1st – has announced that it will return to the US building wire market from mid-year.  Holding a 20-25% market share when it exited the business in 2001 to focus on higher-value products, the company says it will make a limited product range available in western US markets initially from its Chino, CA distribution centre, and move east from its Lebanon, IN and NJ centres as the year progresses.  Outside the US, General Cable also reported its April 12th acquisition of Delphia Produtos Electricos, of Sao Bernardo do Campo, SP in Brazil.  It hopes to capture the growth in the local and regional automotive markets, with the 45-year old company holding a strong share in the ignition cable business.  General Cable is already represented in Brazil with two manufacturing plants at Serra (building wire) and Pocos de Caldas (Al/Cu low- and medium voltage cable and bare conductors). 

### **China** 

**Semis data defies activity on the ground** One of the big conundrums facing anyone wishing to get to grips with the true state of Chinese demand so far this year has been the sharp increase in reported semis production in the face of reports of stocks building amid sluggish consumption.  In the first quarter of this year CNIA data suggests that copper semis output has increased by 22% year on year to 2471.5kt.  This, of course, pales in comparison to apparent consumption calculations which have been artificially boosted as imports are simply piling up in inventories rather than being consumed.  The most obvious explanation for the rise is double co

unting of production. For example, production of wire rod and wire both being counted as semis production, when in fact production of wire is consumption of wire rod and thus only wire rod should be included in the data. This is not the first time that official data has mystified market Metals Market Service Monthly Update - April 2012 Page 6 of 21 Copper Monthly Update watchers, however, with production numbers last year also looking a little on the high side after the CNIA changed the population of their survey group. The key point is that real semis production is nowhere near as upbeat as data suggests. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1100

**Little visibility on near term rod outlook** Major wire rod mills that we are in contact with reported that production in April increased modestly from March, which itself was an improvement from the prior month although year-on-year comparisons remain unfavourable. Power cable and building wire production failed to turn markedly higher, however, and most producers remain concerned about the outlook the next few months in particular. At brass mills, sheet and strip demand turned a little higher in April but again the comparison with a year ago looks rather glib. In fact, some producers have reported output down as much as 10% for the first quarter on a year-on-year basis. Demand for connector strip has been hit by sluggish demand for electrical appliances, while order books for May remain far from full. **Infrastructure spend supports demand** We have noted previously the importance of the power sector to Chinese demand and this seems to be one of the key supporting pillars at present. In the first quarter of this year investment in the power industry increased by 13.2% year on year overall, while investment in power generation and the grid increased by 18.2% and 5.6% respectively. Investment in power generation was mainly driven by investment in hydro power stations and wind farms. One of the key points of the latest five year plan was a focus on energy efficiency and green energy and the expansion in wind farms fits in neatly and also provides a boon to demand for two key reasons; firstly, turbines themselves contain significant amounts of copper but secondly they are often in out of the way places and as such, this increases the requirement for investment in the grid. **Transport picks up pace** Both car production and sales enjoyed a healthy upturn in March, although first quarter sales remain in negative territory on a year-on-year basis. Production in the first quarter expand

ed by 1% but we forecast continued strengthening in both production and sales after a sluggish year in 2011. This should support demand for copper, although this sector accounts for less than 10% of total Chinese demand. **Air conditioner production remains cool** End use demand in the ACR tube sector remains depressed, with air conditioner production contracting by 4.5% in the first quarter of this year and with output down by only 3.4% in March, this does at least suggest that things are not getting worse. An overhang of stocks of finished goods remains a problem but at least we are heading into warmer months in China and in the northern hemisphere in general so a warm spell of weather could quickly eat into unsold units. Meanwhile, a new subsidy programme for energy efficient air conditioners is under discussion and could be introduced later in the year. Clearly this would lift demand but there is also a second implication for copper’s use. More energy efficient applications need to use the most efficient materials and this favours the use of copper and as such, could limit substitution to aluminium. **Further investment in downstream capacity** Golden dragon, the largest copper tube producer in China, has invested 380m RMB to build a 30ktpa ACR tube mill in Luoning county, Luoyang city, Henan province. Construction started recently and the tube mill is expected to be commissioned in 2013/2014. Meanwhile, Ningbo Powerway, a copper and alloy rod producer in China, is building a sheet/strip line with capacity of 40ktpa, which will be commissioned this year. Finally, Wuxi Lineo, a rod and cable company in Jiangsu is investing in a new 120ktpa rod line in Bengbu city, Anhui province in an expansion away from its home province. The name of the new company is Anhu Lineo Copper industry and will use Chinese continuous casting technology for the line which is due to be commissioned later this year. ### **Japan** 

**Capital investment supports economic growth** Japan's economy shrank less than initial estimates suggested in the fourth quarter as companies ramped up capital expenditure.  Expectations are that Japan’s economy will gather momentum and expand from Q2 as exports increase and rebuilding after the earthquake proceeds.  This is supported by the leading Japanese PMI indicators which continue to suggest an economy in recovery with both output and new orders maintaining month on month increases in March, supported by the overall improvement in the global economy and the restoration of supply chains that were damaged by the Thai floods.  This comes despite an unexpected decline in Industrial output in February, as lower overseas demand for cars and electronic goods led to a 1.2% fall month on month according to official figures, against analysts expectations of a 1.3% rise in that month. 

**Automotive subsidies boost wire and cable shipments** Copper wire and cable shipments continued to make gains in March, up 5.9% from a year earlier to an estimated 59,500 tonnes, supported by the robust recovery in orders specifically from the automotive industry.  The reintroduction of Government subsidies for energy efficient or green cars after an 18 months hiatus combined with the extension of tax breaks for fuel-efficient vehicles for another three years (originally set to expire in April 2012) should help to support copper demand further from the automotive sector in the coming months.  Indeed the latest Japanese copper wire and cable shipments indicate that demand from the car sector, rose by 76.2% in March year-on-year to 7,300 tonnes and rose 34.2% to 20,939 tonnes in Q1 2012 over the same period in 2011.  We expect demand from this sector to grow further buoyed by shipments of winding wire for starter motors and other small auto motors and hybrids.  Car and commercial vehicle production growth of 13.8% and 9.6% respectively will also boost connector and brass strip orders, one of the few areas of positive demand for flat rolled copper products in Japan. 

**Construction and power struggle on** In contrast to the automotive sector shipments of wire and cable to both the power and construction sectors were weak, declining, 15.9% and 5% respectively in March year

-on-year and down 4% and 5% in Q1 2012 compared to the previous quarter.  Data suggests that the construction sector may finally be turning the corner in Japan, with housing starts up 7.5% in February from a year earlier and the first rise in six months, an indication that the rebuilding efforts after the earthquake and tsunami in March last year could be feeding through to the construction industry.  However it will take some time for these starts to feed into copper orders as wire and cable is consumed at the end rather than the start of the construction cycle.  Orders for copper sheet and electric wire and cable should recover as reconstruction progresses in the quake-hit areas.

**Brass mills struggle** The latest data from the Japanese brass mills show output is still in the doldrums, declining 9.1% in the first two months of the year compared to levels a year ago.  Domestic production of brass mill semis fell by 8.5% year-on-year to reach 64,076t in February and the association anticipates production of around 67,000t in March, which would represent an 8.3% y-o-y decline for the month and an 8.8% y-o-y contraction in output for Q1 2012.  This comes after a 5% decline in production in the previous year.  The demand for rolled copper products has also remained depressed since autumn 2011 due to weak orders for semi-conductor lead frames and for other electronic products.  We understand that some major sheet & strip manufacturers have temporarily closed their plants.  Production has been hit by off-shoring of production by home appliances manufacturers and a general weakness in demand from the communication equipment segment. 

**Japanese companies offshore semis production** Domestic copper demand growth will be tempered by the slow recovery in the economy and the shift of production by some Japanese entities given the strength of the yen over the past year.  As a consequence, there has been a sharp rise in exports of material to China and other South East Asian countries to meet refined copper requirements at these Japanese owned facilities.  Furukawa Electric announced that it will commission a new electrolytic copper foil factory, located in Taiwan, in July this year.  The facility will produce copper foil suitable for the manufacture of lithium ion batteries.  According to the reports, Furukawa decided to offshore their foil production capacity as the strong yen had limited its competitiveness in the high growth automotive lithium-ion battery market in Taiwan.  In addition, the company expects to see its electricity costs halve in Taiwan.  These account for around 30% of the total cost of electrolytic foil production in Japan.  These costs are unlikely to fall in Japan as the country deals with ongoing power constraints caused by the closure of nuclear power facilities.  A further sign of offshoring by a Japanese company is Sumitomo Electric Indu

stries Ltd’s decision to build a new copper wire rod plant in Thailand. The facility will add 17,000t/m of capacity to the company's current 20,000t/m, which is currently split between its rod mills in Japan and Indonesia. This wire rod will feed growing demand for automotive wiring harnesses and electric motors from the emerging South East Asian car markets. **Chinese scrap demand muted, but secondary capacity grows** Reported

**Codelco tender** Towards the end of the month Codelco issued a tender for 3kt of blister cast as ingots from its Caletones smelter, with 1kt/m available from May to July. In another development the capacity of the Chuquicamata refinery will be increased to 600kt/a by 2014 and, aside from the sale of some anode scrap, Codelco will then no longer participate as a seller in the custom blister market.

## Production news 

**Copper production levels begin to fall away** Confirmation of data from some producers for last year and minor revisions to our forecasts for 2012 have led to lower copper production from mine through to refined, and resulted in a further tightening of what was already expected to be a finely-balanced market.  Mined output for 2011 now stands at 16.234Mt, rather than our March figure of 16.283Mt, while refined output similarly edged down to 19.673Mt from 19.698Mt, and contributed to a marginally higher metal deficit of -133kt vs. our previously shown -93kt.  While this remains small, it adds to the pressure for this year, when we see the deficit now approaching closer to the -200kt mark from March’s -150kt.  Our forecas

t mine output for this year is now down to 16.944Mt from the 16.982Mt we showed in our March report, reflecting the lower than expected output at mines in South America, Asia and Europe.  Meanwhile, refined metal output is down to 20.254Mt from 20.363Mt. 

**Chile hogs the limelight – but not for all the right reasons** With a good selection of the copper mining sector attending the CESCO conference in Chile this month, it is not surprising that all the attention was focused in that region. The poor weather conditions in the upper mountain districts did affect some mining companies.  Anglo American’s Collahuasi operations did not escape even if the losses here were offset by gains at Los Bronces and El Soldado. Severe weather conditions, a fatality in February and a ball mill failure in March were all compounded by the expected lower ore grades, leaving us to expect copper in concentrate output of only 385kt this year vs. 417kt in 2011.  Changing ore profiles at Mantos Blancos should also reduce SxEw mine output this year by 20% (to 27kt vs. 36kt in 2011).  Even though the ramp up at Los Bronces and higher ore grades at El Soldado brought Anglo American Chile’s total output up by 21% this past quarter, to 168.4kt  from 138.8kt in Q1 2011, the impact of Collahuasi’s decline was evident from the comparison with total output during Q4 2011, which was 1% more than Q1 at 170kt. 

**Teck will see output suffer at QB in Q2** In Chile, Teck’s Quebrada Blanca also suffered from adverse weather conditions, but the nature of the operations means that any slide in output will be felt in Q2.  Q1’s output from heap leach and dump leach ore combined rose to 16.9kt from 15.8kt a year ago, but heavy rains affected ore movements and lowered the copper grade in solution, which will show up in next quarter’s output rates.  The company also released details of the proposed QB2 expansion project.  Under the base case view, it will produce 240kt/a copper for the first decade, falling to 200kt/a for its 39-year life of mine, along with 5kt/a contained molybdenum over the LoM, at cash costs of US$1.38/lb.  It is expected to carry a total development cost of US$5.6B, excluding working capital and interest during the construction phase, of which Teck’s own funding requirement would amount to US$4.8B.  We reflect this project in our “probables” category, with 2017 earmarked as initial production.  Elsewhere, Teck’s Highland Valley put higher

Output in terms of recoverable copper was down by more than 56% compared to Q1 2011, at 55.8kt, while net cash costs “soared” to 33c/lb vs. Q1 2011’s -16c/lb, and will continue to suffer at the hands of lower by-product gold credits this year due to low gold ore grades.  Meanwhile, FCX’s Tenke Fungurume property in the DRC continues to exceed expectations, producing 36.3kt recoverable copper compared to 30.4kt in Q1 2011, keeping the plant on track to produce 136kt contained copper this year.  Higher mining and milling rates, though, along with lower cobalt credits, pushed net cash costs up to US$1.25/lb from just 86c/lb in Q1 2011, but should come down to US$1.13/lb, says FCX, for the balance of the year, based on sales volumes and an average cobalt price of US$12/lb.  Aside from the second phase expansion at Tenke, which would see an additional 68kt/a copper capacity become available from late-2013, FCX is also including plans to optimise this first stage of the plant.  Originally designed to operate at 8kt/d ore, the milling section has already shown it can work at 12.2kt/d, and plans under consideration now would increase this to 14kt/d, also by 2013. This optimisation, and the second-phase expansion, comes at a price tag of US$850M and includes mill upgrades, additional mining equipment, a new tankhouse and a sulphuric acid plant expansion.
